processing: Single buds of big-white tea plants are withered on bamboo trays in the sun and then dried over low charcoal heat, with no rolling or firing to fix the green.
harvest_season: Early spring, the first flush of buds, with pre-Qingming picking prized.
appearance_dry: Plump, straight single buds covered in silver-white down.
appearance_liquor: Pale straw-gold, clear, with fine down floating in it.
appearance_wet: Soft, whole, plump buds in pale yellow-green.
taste_profile: Gentle and sweet with honey and floral notes, sometimes a muscat-like lift, and a silky feel from the down.

brewing.notes: Buds release slowly, so give the early steeps more time than a leafy white tea. Cooler water keeps it sweet; a very short first steep will just taste thin.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually as loose current-season tea from the spring first flush. Sellers also offer kept and pressed lots with a stated year, at which point the fresh floral notes give way to honeyed depth. Earlier spring pickings command more money.
description:
This is the all-bud white tea of Fuding, in north-east Fujian near Taimu Shan, which gives it the alias Taimu Silver Needle. Only the bud of a big-white tea plant goes in, and that one rule gives it both its silver look and its price.

The craft looks simple: the buds are spread on bamboo, withered in sun, then dried low over charcoal. Almost everything is decided by the weather and by how long the buds wither. The light handling leaves the down intact and the cup delicate.

Good lots run honeyed and floral, with a silky body and sometimes a muscat-like note, and they stay gentle over many steeps. The usual mistake is impatience: buds need time to give up flavour, so a timid short steep tastes like hot water.

Buy by year and by the look of the leaf: plump, even, downy buds rather than thin or broken ones. Zhenghe makes its own needle in a different style, so tasting the two together is a good way to learn what Fuding means in the cup.
history:
White tea around Taimu Shan has a long literary trail, though not specifically for this modern grade. Scholars link the White Tea Mountain in Lu Yu's Classic of Tea to Taimu, which is an identification and not proof, and Zhou Lianggong's Qing writing names the local Lü Xue Ya.

Modern white tea craft flourished in Qing dynasty Fuding. Records say Chen Huan and Zhang Xiaqin of Bailiu in Diantou moved plants home to propagate in 1857. White tea was exported by the Guangxu years and reached a high point in the early Republic. Local tradition places the mother plant of Fuding Dabai by Hongxue Cave.
